Zacchaeus (Doctrinal)
zak-EE-us
noun
Greek Zakchaios (G2195), from Hebrew Zakkai (H2140) — "pure" or "innocent"; chief tax collector (architelōnēs) in Jericho, short of stature, who climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus and received salvation with restitution (Luke 19:1-10).

📖 Biblical Definition

Zacchaeus is the chief tax collector (Luke 19:2 — Greek architelōnēs, the head of the tax collectors) in Jericho, a man both wealthy and despised. He had grown rich by collecting Roman taxes from his own people — and likely by the standard tax-collector practice of overcharging and pocketing the difference. He was "short of stature," so when Jesus passed through Jericho, Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree to see Him. Christ stopped under the tree, looked up, and addressed him by name: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house" (Luke 19:5). The crowd murmured because Jesus had "gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." Zacchaeus' response is the model of true repentance: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold" (Luke 19:8). NOTE: Zacchaeus does NOT just feel sorry; he MAKES RESTITUTION — and exceeds the OT requirement (Exod 22:1 — fourfold restitution for theft of a sheep, fivefold for an ox; here Zacchaeus voluntarily applies the maximum to all his crooked dealings). Christ pronounces: "This day is salvation come to this house, forasmuch as he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:9-10). The story preaches: (1) Christ specifically seeks out the despised; (2) true conversion produces restitution, not just regret; (3) the marker of saving faith is changed economic behavior; (4) Christ DEFENDS the newly-converted publicly even when the crowd murmurs.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Chief tax collector of Jericho, short of stature, who climbed a sycamore tree to see Christ; received salvation and immediately made fourfold restitution.

expand to see more

ZACCHAEUS, noun. A chief tax collector (Greek architelōnēs) in Jericho, short of stature, who climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus passing through. Luke 19:1-10.

His name means "pure" or "innocent" (Hebrew Zakkai) — an ironic name for a man whose profession involved fraud. His conversion produced immediate restitution: half his goods to the poor, fourfold restitution to any defrauded.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 19:5-7 — "And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house. And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully. And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner."

Luke 19:8-10 — "And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold. And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forasmuch as he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost."

Exodus 22:1 — "If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep."

Luke 19:2 — "And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Zacchaeus is corrupted when the restitution element is treated as optional (regret without repayment becomes the modern norm), or when the children's-song treatment ("Zacchaeus was a wee little man") leaves the canonical adult-conversion theology unread.

expand to see more

Restitution-optional theology. Modern evangelism often presents salvation as "believe in Jesus and your sins are forgiven," with restitution to wronged parties treated as optional follow-up. But the canonical Zacchaeus story is explicit: Christ pronounces "salvation has come to this house" AFTER Zacchaeus commits to restitution, not before. Christ does not require restitution as the GROUND of salvation (Christ's righteousness alone justifies), but Zacchaeus' restitution is the EVIDENCE of true conversion. True repentance includes making right what we can. "If I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold" is not the optional behavior of a generous convert; it is the natural fruit of saving faith.

Children's-song flattening. "Zacchaeus was a wee little man / and a wee little man was he" is a charming children's song that has, for many American adults, replaced the canonical story in their memory. The actual text is theologically sophisticated: a chief tax collector (powerful, wealthy, despised) receives Christ, restructures his entire economic life in one statement, and is pronounced "a son of Abraham" (covenantally restored) by Christ Himself. The children's-song layer should not eclipse the adult-conversion theology underneath.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Zakchaios (G2195), Hebrew Zakkai (H2140) — "pure"; chief tax collector of Jericho whose conversion produced fourfold restitution.

expand to see more

Greek Zakchaios (G2195) — Zacchaeus; transliteration of Hebrew Zakkai

Hebrew Zakkai (H2140) — "pure" or "innocent" — ironic name for a chief tax collector

Greek architelōnēs (G754) — chief tax collector; appears only at Luke 19:2 (referring to Zacchaeus)

Restitution: half his goods to the poor + fourfold to any defrauded — exceeds the OT maximum (Exod 22:1)

Usage

"Christ specifically sought out Zacchaeus by name in the sycamore tree — the despised are precisely whom He came to save."

"Zacchaeus' conversion produced immediate fourfold restitution; true repentance includes making right what we can."

"Salvation has come to this house — pronounced by Christ AFTER, not before, Zacchaeus committed to restitution."
